content:
CNN reports that Rep. Jamie Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week challenging the company’s explanation for removing ICEBlock from the App Store last year. Here are the details.

ICEBlock removal once again under scrutiny

According to CNN, Apple sent a letter to Rep. Jamie Raskin last July explaining its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store, and Raskin has now responded with new questions about the company’s justification.

For context, ICEBlock was one of the most prominent apps that allowed users to report and track ICE activity in their area. The app rapidly rose in popularity during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, growing from around 20,000 users to roughly one million within weeks.

As its popularity skyrocketed, ICEBlock became the target of the US government, with then-Attorney General Pam Bondi publicly calling for Apple to remove the app and warning its developer that he could face prosecution.

Following pressure from the DOJ, Apple removed it and several similar apps from the App Store, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents. The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

This, in turn, prompted Raskin to investigate whether the Trump administration had pressured Apple and Google into removing ICE-tracking apps, and what impact those removals may have had on constitutionally protected speech.

As part of that investigation, CNN reports that Apple sent Raskin a letter last July explaining why it removed ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store.

From CNN:

Apple says its decision to remove ICEBlock and similar platforms from the app store last year was prompted by concerns — including those raised by the Trump administration — about agent safety following a fatal shooting that left two detainees dead at a Dallas Immigration and Customs Enforcement office.

Apple’s explanation came in a July letter to Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, who earlier this year launched an investigation into the Justice Department’s role in the removal of the apps from Apple’s and Google’s app stores and the impact on constitutionally protected speech. The letter has not previously been reported.

CNN says that Apple’s letter to Raskin also mentioned that the company approved ICEBlock in April 2025, after developer Joshua Aaron addressed what Apple referred to as “certain user privacy concerns.”

Apple also reportedly said it continued to monitor news coverage and criticism of the app in the months that followed, ultimately deciding to remove ICEBlock and similar apps after concluding they violated its App Store guidelines by providing “precise location information about ICE officers,” which could potentially be used for targeted attacks.

Apple also cited concerns raised by Bondi after the Dallas shooting, as well as comments from FBI Director Kash Patel that the shooter had searched for apps that tracked ICE agents’ locations.

According to Apple, those concerns, together with what it described as a broader increase in ICE activity and threats against agents, prompted the company to conduct a new review of ICEBlock.

Raskin pushes back

According to CNN, Raskin sent a letter to Apple this week further questioning the company’s justification for removing ICEBlock and similar apps from the App Store.

Top comment by Doug

Sounds like grandstanding. It was brought to Apple's attention that the app was being used to target ICE and the result was some serious clashes with some very bad outcomes. So they choose to remove them. Sort of like how Facebook, twitter, etc... shut down Trump after Jan 6th. It wasn't ideal but they had the right to do it.

Nothing to see here....move along...

From CNN:

CNN also notes that Raskin disputed Apple’s reliance on the Dallas shooting, arguing that the gunman did not need an ICE-tracking app to locate a fixed government facility and reportedly found the address using “an app that comes standard on Apple devices.”

He also pointed to other navigation apps that remain available on the App Store despite providing real-time information about law enforcement locations, and asked Apple to conduct a new independent review of the removals and provide a full list of apps it removed in response to concerns raised by the DOJ.
